common_name: Batik Bearded Iris (Striking Purple-and-White Streaked Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Batik is a striking and unusual bearded iris cultivar named for its irregular, brushed and streaked pattern of deep purple over a white ground, giving each ruffled flower a hand-dyed, painterly look unlike the more uniform color patterns of most bearded iris. Its bold, unmistakable appearance has made it a long-standing favorite for gardeners wanting a conversation-piece iris that stands out in a mixed spring border. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans to keep the clump vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Superstition Bearded Iris (Dramatic Near-Black Velvet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Superstition is one of the darkest bearded iris cultivars available, with velvety, near-black purple flowers so deeply saturated they appear black in most light, held on tall, well-branched stems above broad sword-like foliage. Its dramatic, almost mysterious color has made it one of the most sought-after dark iris for gardeners building a moon garden or dramatic color-themed border, where it provides striking contrast against pale or silver companion plants. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Popcorn Drift Rose (Compact Groundcover Rose with Creamy-Yellow Blooms)

planting.note: Plant container-grown roses in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Popcorn Drift's low, spreading habit and repeat bloom without deadheading make it a low-maintenance groundcover and border rose.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, spacing plants to allow the low, spreading habit to fill in as a groundcover without crowding. Popcorn Drift is part of the Drift series of compact groundcover roses, a cross between full-sized groundcover roses and miniature roses that combines the disease resistance and toughness of landscape roses with a scale small enough for foundation plantings, borders, and containers. It produces clusters of small, semi-double, creamy-white to pale yellow flowers with a soft popcorn-like fullness continuously from late spring through frost, self-cleaning without the need for deadheading. Like other Drift roses it has strong resistance to black spot and other common rose diseases, needing only a hard cutback in late winter to renew growth and shape, making it one of the lowest-maintenance flowering shrubs available for sunny beds and slopes.
sources: Star Roses and Plants — Drift rose series notes

common_name: UpTick Coreopsis (Large-Flowered Long-Blooming Compact Tickseed Series)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; UpTick blooms the first year and continues nonstop through summer into fall without deadheading.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid heavy, poorly drained ground where coreopsis crowns are prone to rot over winter. UpTick is a vegetatively propagated coreopsis series bred for unusually large flowers, up to three inches across, on compact, well-branched plants that bloom continuously from late spring through frost without deadheading, a marked improvement over the smaller flowers and shorter bloom window of older seed-grown tickseed cultivars. Its dense, mounded habit and strong repeat bloom make it a reliable performer at the front of a sunny border, and established plants are notably heat- and drought-tolerant, thriving in the same lean, well-drained conditions native Coreopsis grandiflora prefers in the wild. Deadheading is not required to keep it flowering, though shearing lightly midseason can refresh a tired-looking plant.
sources: Darwin Perennials — UpTick coreopsis series notes
